Education & Research Breast Enlargement Research Library An independent reading guide to external research and patient information. These studies and source publications are not Quantum Health research. Home/Education & Research/Breast Enlargement Research Library External research, clearly attributedQuantum Health provides educational summaries, not original clinical research. Publication does not prove effectiveness. Read each source in context, check its date and jurisdiction, and distinguish a registered protocol from a completed review. PubMed study summaries · Search PMC records · Cochrane systematic reviews and protocols · U.S. FDA — regulator guidance · NHS — UK patient information · healthdirect — Australian health information · Cleveland Clinic — external patient education · American Society of Plastic Surgeons · British Association of Plastic, Reconstructive and Aesthetic Surgeons · British Association of Aesthetic Plastic Surgeons · StatPearls — NCBI Bookshelf clinical review · MedlinePlus — National Library of Medicine · Wikipedia — enlargement encyclopedia reference · Wikipedia — augmentation encyclopedia reference PubMed: topic-grouped study findingsThis page collects peer-reviewed research on breast enlargement — surgical and non-surgical — indexed in PubMed, the US National Library of Medicine’s database of biomedical literature. In October 2026 we searched PubMed using title and abstract terms covering breast augmentation, breast enlargement, fat transfer and autologous fat grafting, non-surgical enlargement, breast implants and breast fillers. Of 77 unique records retrieved, the most relevant are summarised here, grouped by topic, with a link to each original PubMed record.What the literature shows in brief: breast augmentation with implants remains one of the most frequently performed aesthetic operations worldwide, with predictable volume but real complication and revision rates. Autologous fat grafting is the best-supported route to lasting volume without an implant, but the gain is modest and complications occur in roughly a quarter of cases in the largest systematic review. External vacuum expansion has produced true tissue growth in small studies, but demands weeks of daily device wear. Injectable fillers are not approved for breast enlargement, and published case series document serious complications. Creams, pills and most devices have no credible supporting trials. How this page was compiledSearches were run on PubMed (National Library of Medicine, USA) in October 2026 using title/abstract terms: “breast augmentation”, “breast enlargement”, (“fat transfer” OR “autologous fat grafting” OR “fat grafting”) AND breast augmentation, (“non-surgical” OR filler OR PRP OR “platelet-rich plasma”) AND breast enlargement, and breast implants AND (augmentation OR enlargement). 77 unique records were retrieved; the studies most relevant to breast enlargement are summarised below. Summaries use abstract-level data — consult the full article and current guidelines before drawing clinical conclusions. Inclusion here is not an endorsement of any study or treatment. Evidence at a glance The headline findings, by question Each row links to the PubMed record behind the finding. The headline findings, by question QuestionWhat the published evidence showsKey studies Does fat transfer enlarge breasts?Yes — modestly. The largest systematic review (35 studies, 3,757 women) reported an average 58% fat retention from about 300 mL injected per breast — roughly one cup — with a 27.8% overall complication rate and 92% average patient satisfaction.Seth 2024 (PMID 37166041) Is fat transfer better than implants?The only randomised trial identified found implants gave more evident and durable augmentation (87.5% vs 70% “excellent” aesthetic outcomes), while fat grafting produced more natural-looking results and better correction of chest-wall deformity.Gentile 2026 (PMID 40908320) Can a vacuum device enlarge breasts without surgery?A 2000 study reported a stable 55% average size increase after 10 weeks of daily external expansion (10–12 h/day); MRI confirmed growth of fat and fibroglandular tissue. Evidence remains limited and largely developer-led.Khouri 2000 (PMID 10845308); Kardorff 2004 (PMID 16285326) Do breast fillers work — and are they safe?Hyaluronic acid gel was briefly authorised for breast use in Europe (2008), then withdrawn worldwide after side effects. A 31-patient complication series found 88.9% of conservatively treated aquafilling cases needed reoperation. Regulators advise against fillers for breast enlargement.Siebert 2014 (PMID 24507861); Gierej 2023 (PMID 37721627); Jeyaratnam 2021 (PMID 34849315) How often do implants need revision?Reported revision rates after primary augmentation are as high as 36%, most commonly for capsular contracture, implant malposition and ptosis of the ageing breast.Denney 2021 (PMID 34121945) Is “breast implant illness” established?Systemic symptoms attributed to implants are widely reported, but a 2024 Danish review notes the correlation with implants is not established, evidence is limited, and it is not a recognised diagnosis.Borhani-Khomani 2024 (PMID 38808767) How common is augmentation worldwide?ISAPS 14-year global data show breast augmentation consistently among the top five surgical aesthetic procedures. Implant removal has been the fastest-growing procedure since 2015 (+46.3% over five years).Triana 2024 (PMID 39103642) Study figures describe the groups studied and may not apply to any individual. Evidence and regulatory positions change — check the linked records and current regulator guidance before acting. Fat transfer (autologous fat grafting)Fat transfer removes fat by liposuction from another body area and injects it into the breast. It is the best-documented route to real, lasting volume without an implant — but the gain is modest, and the evidence base, while growing, is still dominated by retrospective series rather than controlled trials. Fat transfer studies What fat-grafting research reports What fat-grafting research reports StudyDesignWhat it found Seth I, et al. 2024 — Plast Reconstr Surg (PMID 37166041)Systematic review: 35 studies, 3,757 womenAverage 300 mL injected per breast; 58% volume retention (range 44–83%); 27.8% overall complication rate, fat necrosis the most common (43.7% of complications); radiologic fat necrosis 9.4%, calcification 1.2%; 92% average satisfaction at one year. Gentile P. 2026 — Aesthetic Plast Surg (PMID 40908320)Randomised open-label trial: 95 implants vs 90 lipofilling87.5% of implant patients vs 70% of lipofilling patients had excellent aesthetic outcomes at 12 months. Implant results were significantly more durable; lipofilling results were judged more natural and improved pectus excavatum. Both were safe and effective. Voglimacci M, et al. 2015 — Aesthetic Surg J (PMID 25908697)Systematic review: 42 articlesEvidence mostly low level (one level-2 study). Two cancers among 2,023 patients (0.09%) with insufficient follow-up for long-term conclusions. Concludes registries with proper follow-up are needed. Leopardi D, et al. 2014 — ANZ J Surg (PMID 23656507)Systematic review vs implant comparatorsNo comparative studies were found. Fat necrosis, cysts and lumps were the most common complications; reabsorption occurs mainly in the first 12 months; efficacy could not be determined from the available evidence. Hivernaud V, et al. 2015 — Aesthetic Plast Surg (PMID 26085223)Technique reviewHigh resorption remains the central problem of large-volume grafting; refinements in harvesting and graft preparation aim to improve fat viability and long-term success. Coleman SR, Saboeiro AP. 2015 — Clin Plast Surg (PMID 26116935)Technique reviewThe 2009 ASPS Fat Graft Task Force concluded fat grafting may be considered for breast augmentation, with results dependent on technique and surgeon expertise. Finzi E. 2003 — Dermatol Surg (PMID 12930335)Retrospective record reviewBreast enlargement occurred in 43% of patients after tumescent liposuction of other body areas; 30% gained one cup size or more — an incidental, redistribution-based effect. Seth I, et al. 2023 — Gland Surg (PMID 36761486)Method paper: hybrid augmentationProposes a preoperative formula to estimate fat-graft volume when combining implants with lipofilling (hybrid breast augmentation). Non-surgical enlargement: external expansionExternal vacuum expansion devices (bra-like systems worn for hours a day) aim to grow tissue through controlled mechanical stretch. Small studies report measurable growth; the regimens are demanding, and critics have questioned measurement consistency. Questions About this research page What is PubMed, and why use it? PubMed is the US National Library of Medicine’s free index of biomedical literature, covering thousands of peer-reviewed journals. Searching it gives a structured, reproducible view of what has actually been studied — rather than what is advertised. Does listing a study mean we recommend its findings? No. Listing means the study is part of the published evidence base. Individual studies vary in quality — a small case report carries far less weight than a systematic review or randomised trial. Nothing on this page is a recommendation for any individual. Why do study findings sometimes disagree? Different designs, patient groups, surgical techniques, measurement methods and eras produce different results. Systematic reviews that pool many studies sit at the top of the evidence ladder; single-centre case series sit lower. How current is this page? The PubMed search was run in October 2026. New studies are indexed continuously — check PubMed for the latest work, and look for updated systematic reviews and regulator statements. Where can I read the full articles? Each link opens the study’s PubMed record with its abstract. Many full texts sit behind journal subscriptions; ask a librarian, university library or your clinician for access, and treat any claim you cannot verify with caution. Educational information only — not medical adviceThis page summarises published research for general education. It cannot account for your health, anatomy or circumstances, and it does not recommend any treatment. Study figures may not transfer to individuals. Decisions about breast enlargement should be made with a qualified, registered clinician after proper assessment. If you notice a new breast lump or any urgent symptom, seek medical care promptly. Where the Cochrane evidence runs outCochrane has published no systematic review of cosmetic breast augmentation as a procedure — no review of augmentation techniques, implant placement planes, satisfaction after cosmetic surgery, or long-term outcomes in women who had implants for enlargement rather than reconstruction. The completed reviews here were written for breast reduction and post-mastectomy reconstruction; their findings are evidence about those settings, not direct evidence about augmentation for cosmetic purposes.There is also no Cochrane review of fat transfer or autologous fat grafting for cosmetic breast enlargement (the reconstruction protocol was withdrawn in 2021), none of silicone gel implants used for cosmetic purposes, none of breast uplift (mastopexy), none of gynaecomastia surgery in men, and none of the non-surgical options discussed elsewhere on this site — fillers, platelet-rich plasma, threads or biostimulators. Absence of a Cochrane review does not mean a treatment works or does not work; it means the question has not been systematically synthesised at this level, and other evidence must be weighed instead. British Association of Plastic, Reconstructive and Aesthetic SurgeonsThis page works through the patient guide published by the British Association of Plastic, Reconstructive and Aesthetic Surgeons (BAPRAS) — the four-part guide to breast augmentation (bilateral breast augmentation, or BBA): what the operation is, how to choose a surgeon, implant techniques, the complications that can occur and the long-term consequences. Every part is summarised here and linked to the original, so the current wording can always be checked at source.BAPRAS describes breast enlargement as a potentially life-enhancing procedure — but also as a big decision: major surgery with potential risks, and a result that cannot be guaranteed. The guide was edited by Lee Martin and Emma de Sousa, with contributions from Julie Doughty, Paul Harris, Mark Henley, Nigel Mercer, Charles Nduka, Mary O’Brien, Caroline Payne and Ruth Waters, and was last updated in 2021. A printed copy of the guide is available from the BAPRAS secretariat, and a PDF is published alongside the online version.This summary is educational. It does not replace the discussion you should have with your own surgeon, and it does not constitute medical advice or a recommendation of any procedure, surgeon or clinic. The four-part guide What the BAPRAS guide covers From the first consultation to the decisions that stay with you for decades. The decision Who the guide is for, what breast augmentation can and cannot achieve, and why realistic expectations matter. Consultation & cooling-off How to seek a consultation, what happens at it, and why a cooling-off period of at least two weeks is required. Implant techniques Incisions, placement behind the breast or muscle, dual plane, and how implant type, size, shape and texture are chosen. The operation Anaesthetic, time in hospital, recovery week by week, and how scars typically evolve over the first year. Complications Reported frequencies for bleeding, infection, capsular contracture, sensation change and rupture — plus BIA-ALCL and breast implant illness. Long-term questions Mammography with implants, alternatives such as lipofilling and uplift surgery, and the national implant registry. What this page is — and is notThis is a condensed, section-by-section summary of BAPRAS patient information written for people considering breast enlargement in the United Kingdom. Figures such as complication frequencies are those published in the guide; UK practice, funding rules and professional registers differ between countries, so local standards still apply wherever a procedure is performed.Nothing here is a personal assessment of suitability. That can only be done in a consultation with a qualified, registered surgeon who examines you. What breast augmentation isBreast augmentation (bilateral breast augmentation or BBA) is an operation to enlarge the breasts, usually by inserting an implant beneath the breast to make it look larger. It can enlarge breasts that have always been small, and it can also fill out breasts that used to be larger — for example breasts that have emptied out after pregnancy. The procedure reshapes breasts to some extent and can be used to correct breasts that are of unequal size.An alternative to enlargement with an implant is fat transfer, sometimes called lipomodelling, lipofilling or fat grafting: fat taken from elsewhere on the body is injected into the breast area. Fat transfer may be appropriate for a few people but is not suitable for all, often requires more than one episode of surgery, and can also be combined with an implant augmentation.Patients who have breast augmentation tend to be pleased with the results, but the guide is explicit that expectations must be realistic. You need to understand what can and cannot be achieved, the limitations of surgery, and the long-term consequences of having breast implants. Next steps Getting to a decision The BAPRAS guide sets out a deliberate, unhurried path from first enquiry to the operating table. 01 Find a surgeonYour GP may be able to suggest surgeons locally, or you can approach a private hospital or clinic directly. If you do, make sure your initial consultation is with the surgeon who will actually do the operation. Your surgeon will normally seek permission to write to your GP afterwards. 02 Attend a full consultationYou will be asked what is bothering you about your breasts and what you expect from surgery, must share your full medical history, and will be examined with measurements taken. Discussion follows about implant shapes, possible sizes and the position of the pockets behind your existing breast tissue. A consultation fee is normal. 03 See the likely resultSome surgeons use implant sizers in a bra, others 3D photography. This is only a guide — the same implant can look very different in different people. You should be told about the operation, the expected outcome and the possible risks and complications. 04 Take the cooling-off periodYou should be given a cooling-off period of at least two weeks before surgery and offered a second consultation. You should not feel rushed into surgery — if you are, walk away. Why there is a cooling-off periodBreast augmentation is a lifetime commitment and must not be considered a one-stop permanent solution. You need to be making the appropriate choice and understand all the implications of the surgery you are considering — including that you will need revision surgery as the years go by, and that you must be prepared personally and financially for this.Nobody needs an urgent breast augmentation. If you are not offered a cooling-off period, or you are put under pressure to proceed, the guide’s advice is simple: walk away. Check the register at gmc-uk.org using “Check a doctor’s registration status”. Under “Status” they should be listed as “Registered with a license to practise; this doctor is on the specialist register”. Surgeons may also be registered with the Association of Breast Surgery (ABS), BAAPS and/or BAPRAS — members of these organisations hold a standard set of recognised qualifications. It is perfectly reasonable to ask about a surgeon’s experience and qualifications. Internet searchesInformation found through search engines may be promotional in nature; some surgeons and services pay for their listing. A prominent listing is a measure of marketing ability, not of service quality. CostAn approximate cost should be obtainable from your local private hospital or the surgeon’s secretary before your consultation, and you should expect to pay a fee for the consultation itself. After your consultation(s), if you plan to go ahead, you should be given a written quote for the planned care. Deposits and inducementsAvoid any deal asking for a non-refundable deposit, and do not accept a financial inducement or time-limited deal — even offering to refund the consultation fee if you proceed with surgery is considered an inducement and is against GMC guidance. Package pricesIt is appropriate to be offered a package covering the whole process and the cost of treating any complications arising in the initial weeks after surgery. You should be told exactly what the package includes. The cheapest deal may not be the best: cosmetic surgery is a significant financial commitment, and you will need to pay for further surgery in the future. NHS fundingCosmetic breast augmentation is not available on the NHS, so you will normally consult and pay privately. Exceptional circumstances can include very uneven breasts (a significant difference in size), having no breasts, or treatment as part of a breast reconstruction care plan — your GP can explain the rules in your area. Surgery abroadIf you go abroad for breast augmentation, be aware that on return to the UK only emergency complications will be dealt with by the NHS. Summarised from the BAPRAS patient guide. Cosmetic-surgery funding, regulation and professional registers differ between countries — verify the current position in your own jurisdiction. Implant techniquesBreast enlargement involves placing an implant under the breast tissue to increase the size and shape of the breast. Implants are usually inserted through an incision under the breast at the crease, but they can also be placed through an incision in the armpit or around the nipple.Behind the breast (sub-glandular)Placing the implant behind the breast, on top of the chest wall muscle, is considered the simplest of the available enlargement procedures and is less likely to cause significant discomfort. This route is also effective for patients with some drooping of the breasts.Behind the muscle (sub-muscular)Placing the implant behind the breast muscle gives more padding or coverage for the implant. This can help slender patients and those with very little breast tissue, because it reduces the chances of being able to feel or see the implant under the breast tissue.Dual plane augmentationSurgeons often combine the two routes, placing the implant partly behind the breast and partly behind the muscle, to try to give the benefits of both — this is called a dual plane augmentation. If implants are inserted behind the muscle they are likely to move when the muscle contracts; this is called animation and is normal. Your surgeon will advise which placement is appropriate for you. What the operation involvesBefore and after photographs should be taken for your clinical record, to help you and your surgeon plan the operation and assess the result. Your face is not included and you will be asked for consent; if your surgeon wants to use the images for teaching or publication, they must ask for specific additional consent.Breast enlargement surgery takes about one-and-a-half hours and is usually done under general anaesthetic. You may be able to go home the same day, but many patients spend one night in hospital. Postoperative pain should be well controlled: your chest may feel tight and your breasts and ribs may be tender. You will be mobile from day one and should be back to full exercise within six weeks, with one to two weeks off work recommended.At first the breasts may look high and the skin tight; this tends to settle over the first six weeks, but the long-term result takes three to four months as a more natural shape emerges. Most patients are pleased with their surgery, though some find the new shape difficult to get used to. Scars are typically quite red for the first six weeks, change to purple over the next three months and then fade to white. Most patients form good-quality scars, but abnormal scarring can occur. Implant techniques Choosing the implant Choosing the implant DecisionWhat the BAPRAS guide says Fill materialThe outer shell of all implants is made of silicone, and some have an additional polyurethane coating. The shell is filled with either silicone gel or saline. Implants have been used since the 1960s and the evidence suggests they are safe. Most patients are offered silicone gel-filled implants — they tend to feel the most natural, come in a range of shapes and are durable. Saline implants feel less natural, folds or ripples may be more visible, and they carry a risk of deflation. All other filler materials have been withdrawn for use in the UK. Ask your surgeon exactly which type and manufacturer will be used, and why. SizeImplants are supplied by volume, and it is not possible to guarantee a cup size. Your surgeon assesses your chest wall, your existing breast tissue and how much skin is available, then indicates an appropriate range — your own view matters, because in most patients a range of sizes could be used. The larger the implant and the slimmer you are, the less natural the result; an implant out of proportion with your frame is more likely to cause complications such as drooping, stretching of the breast tissue and being more easily felt. ShapeImplants are round or teardrop (anatomical). Round implants give more volume at the top of the breast and are as wide as they are tall. With teardrop implants the width and height can be chosen separately, giving more control of the eventual shape. Both come in varying degrees of projection; your surgeon discusses the best shape for your frame and desired outcome. TextureSurfaces are smooth or textured, in degrees from very fine to coarse; some implants have a foamy polyurethane coating. Texturing exists to reduce capsular contracture (evidence is strongest when the implant is placed in front of the muscle) and to reduce unwanted movement or rotation — so anatomical implants tend to be textured, while rotation of a round implant is not noticeable. A textured surface is linked to the uncommon BIA-ALCL; smooth implants currently have no such link. Smooth implants are almost always round, move within the breast and take several months to settle, and can slip sideways (lateral displacement) or drop below the crease (bottoming out). The choice is not straightforward — your surgeon should help decide. Silicone safetyImplants are made from medical-grade silicone. Small quantities of silicone can be taken up by the body and found in breast tissue and sometimes the armpit lymph glands; occasionally the body forms inflammation and extra tissue around silicone deposits (silicone granuloma). If the shell fails, the gel often keeps its shape and the appearance may not change — ruptures are frequently discovered by accident while investigating another breast problem, though they can cause lumpiness or a change in shape. A confirmed rupture is treated by removal of the implants, with replacement possible at the same or a later operation. There is no association between breast augmentation and breast cancer. The three most important decisions are implant size, shape and placement. Summarised from the BAPRAS implant techniques guide. What complications can occur?All operations are associated with risks. Serious complications are uncommon with breast augmentation, occurring in less than 1 in 100 operations. The figures below are those published in the BAPRAS guide. Reported frequencies Risks and how often they occur Risks and how often they occur ComplicationWhat the BAPRAS guide says Serious complications overallUncommon — less than 1 in 100 breast augmentation operations. Bleeding (haematoma)Less than 1 in 100. Usually immediately after surgery, occasionally up to two weeks later. The breast becomes very swollen and tight and you return to theatre to have the blood removed and the bleeding stopped; the implant can be retained. Expect an extra night in hospital and more bruising than usual. Haematoma can increase the risk of later capsular contracture. InfectionLess than 1 in 1000. Usually apparent over the first two or three weeks: swelling, tenderness, redness, wound discharge and a raised temperature. Antibiotics sometimes settle a mild infection, but most established infections around the implant require removal — a new implant cannot be inserted immediately, and three to six months should pass before re-insertion. Your package price should cover treatment of bleeding or infection. Capsular contractureThe body forms a scar capsule around every implant; when it contracts the breast feels firmer, and may become round or tender. Noticeable firmness occurs in up to 1 in 10 of all breast augmentations, but most of those patients do not need revision surgery. Options include living with it (safe), releasing the capsule (capsulotomy) or removing it (capsulectomy) with a new implant — but scar tissue can return in at least half of people having secondary surgery. Capsular contracture is the most common reason for re-operation, and once it has happened it is likely to recur in 1 in 2 cases. Re-operation for any reasonAbout 1% (1 in 100) per year — so after 10 years, about 10 in every 100 women will have had more surgery. Changes in sensationSome alteration of sensation is usual, most often numbness and oversensitivity of the nipples. Oversensitivity gradually settles, usually over several months. Around 1 in 5 patients have a reduction in nipple sensation; recovery can take up to 12 months, and 1 in 10 patients have some permanent numbness. Feeling or seeing the implantIt is common to feel the implant, especially in slim patients or those with little breast tissue; this is an inevitable consequence of the operation and does not improve with time. Ripples or folds may become visible leaning forwards. Small amounts of your own fat can be injected (lipomodelling) to improve the situation in some patients. A marked crease can be a sign of capsular contracture. Implant failure (rupture)The shell can eventually fail. The American Core study (FDA update, 2011) found 1 in 10 implants had ruptured at 10 years, and it is estimated half of all breast implants may rupture by 15 years. Rupture is often contained within the body’s own capsule (silent rupture) and does not appear harmful; some patients notice a change in size, shape or consistency, a lump or swelling. A scan is usually performed and, if rupture is suggested, removal and exchange is advised. There is no universally agreed replacement schedule, and exchange before ten years is unusual — if you have noticed no change, no regular follow-up or scans are needed. AsymmetrySome asymmetry between breasts is normal and perfect symmetry is not an achievable goal; asymmetry may appear more pronounced after surgery. A larger implant in the smaller breast improves the volume difference only, not other differences such as nipple position. Implants can also settle differently in their pockets. Wide cleavageImplants are positioned centrally behind the nipples and will not improve a naturally wide cleavage — with sub-muscular placement the cleavage can even appear wider. Breasts and implants falling to the sides when you lie down is normal. Stretch marks and veinsStretch marks may develop after surgery, especially with larger implants, and veins may become more noticeable on the breast surface. Ptosis (sagging)Breasts will sag with time because augmented breasts are larger and heavier — the larger the implant, the more the breast will droop. They may also “bottom out”, meaning the implant sits lower, below the nipple rather than above it. Pregnancy and breastfeedingImplants do not interfere with the ability to breastfeed. There is some evidence that the amount of milk produced by some women with implants is reduced, and no evidence of increased illness in children of women with silicone gel implants. Pregnancy and breastfeeding may adversely affect the shape of the breast. Other reasons for re-operationSome patients choose re-augmentation with larger implants as time goes by; augmented breasts change shape with time, pregnancy and weight fluctuation; teardrop-shaped implants can rotate behind the breast (usually rotating back by themselves or being gently pushed back, but repeated rotation needs re-operation, especially with large implants correcting droop); and intermittent swelling around an implant may lead to scans, further tests or implant replacement. Who pays for future treatmentMany of these long-term problems will not be covered by the package bought at the time of surgery, and you should not expect the NHS to provide future treatment. You must be prepared to pay for consultations, scans and further surgery if needed. Frequency figures are those published in the BAPRAS patient guide (updated 2021) and describe breast augmentation generally; individual risk depends on your anatomy, the technique used and your health. Breast Implant Associated Anaplastic Large Cell Lymphoma (BIA-ALCL)Since 2016, anaplastic large cell lymphoma in association with breast implants has been recognised by the World Health Organization. The risk is small. It is not a breast cancer but a type of cancer associated with the scar tissue (capsule) the body lays down around an implant. Cases have occurred between 2 and 28 years after implant insertion, with an average of 8 years, and it most likely presents as swelling around the implant (a seroma) causing an increase in breast size. It can usually be treated successfully by removing the implant and the surrounding capsule.Because it is uncommon, international organisations share data on the condition. Most cases worldwide have occurred in women with textured breast implants, with higher numbers where the texture is coarser — so ask your surgeon for the most up-to-date recommendations. Breast implants continue to hold safety approval from government organisations such as the UK MHRA and the USA FDA and remain used in breast reconstruction after cancer worldwide.Breast Implant Illness (BII)Breast Implant Illness is a term used by some patients who experience symptoms they feel are connected to their silicone implants — tiredness, “brain fog”, joint aches, immune-related symptoms, sleep disturbance, depression, hormonal issues, headaches, hair loss, chills, rash and neurological issues. BII is not a medical diagnosis, there is no proven association with breast implants, and there is currently no scientific evidence confirming the proposed link or any diagnostic test for the condition; research continues. Some patients report improvement after implant removal, but not all do. The UK government guidance on BII symptoms and the FDA’s breast-implant risk pages are referenced in the guide. Long-term consequences and alternativesMammography and screeningImplants push your natural breasts forward and do not make it harder to examine your breasts for lumps, but they do interfere with mammography: X-rays cannot pass through the implant, so some breast tissue is obscured. UK breast screening starts at age 50. If you are called for a screening mammogram you must tell the service you have implants — they may scan you at a different centre and take special views. The more of your total breast volume that is implant, the greater the problem, so a breast augmentation reduces the sensitivity of a future mammogram. Some patients pay privately for MRI screening instead to avoid these issues.Myths and routine replacementIt is not unsafe to sunbathe or to fly in an aeroplane with implants — neither presents a problem. There is no need to massage breast implants, and this is not recommended with modern textured-surface implants. Routine replacement after a specified time is not recommended: replacement is advised only if you are unhappy with the appearance or have developed a problem.Alternatives: lipofilling and breast upliftThe only alternative surgical technique to enlarge the breast is lipofilling (fat transfer): fat is removed by liposuction from the hips, thighs or tummy and injected into the breast area. Only a relatively small amount can be injected, so multiple operations are usually needed for a worthwhile effect; some fat is absorbed in the first weeks, but fat lasting beyond that brings permanent enlargement. It is more gradual than implant surgery and avoids an implant, but the surgeon cannot be sure how effective it will be and results are variable. Your own fat is the only substance that can be safely injected into the breast — other materials have been tried and withdrawn. Do not allow anyone to inject anything other than your own fat.If you are bothered by droopiness but happy with your breast size, you do not need an augmentation — you may be offered a breast uplift (mastopexy), which lifts the nipple and breast tissue and tightens the skin, with incisions around the areola and possibly vertically and under the breast. Scarring is more obvious than with augmentation alone and no implant is used, but uplifted breasts tend to droop again with time and gravity, and often seem smaller afterwards despite little or no tissue removal. Mild droopiness can be improved by augmentation alone; where both volume loss and droopiness are a problem, augmentation and mastopexy may be discussed as one operation or in two stages — usually best done one at a time, though sometimes performed together after careful planning and counselling, with results that are not always entirely predictable in size and shape.Breast Implant RegistryIn the UK there is a national Breast and Cosmetic Implant Registry, administered by NHS Digital, recording every implant placed or removed with patient details, the organisation and the surgeon. Its main aim is to trace and inform affected patients if a failed implant is ever recalled, and to identify possible trends and complications relating to specific implants. Entry requires your consent, and you are strongly recommended to agree to the register if you have implant-based surgery — for your own protection and that of others. Quick answers Questions the BAPRAS guide answers Can my surgeon guarantee a cup size? No. Implants are supplied by volume and it is not possible to guarantee a cup size. Your surgeon assesses your chest wall, existing breast tissue and available skin, then indicates an appropriate range of sizes — in most patients a range could be used, and your own preference decides where in that range to sit. Do breast implants have to be replaced after a set number of years? No. There is no universally agreed replacement schedule, and exchange before ten years is unusual. If you have noticed no change you do not need regular follow-up or scans. You should still be prepared — personally and financially — for further surgery at some point, since about 1% of patients have a re-operation each year. Is breast enlargement available on the NHS? Cosmetically, no — you would consult and pay as a private patient. Exceptions include very uneven breasts, having no breasts, or treatment within a reconstruction care plan. If you have surgery abroad, only emergency complications will be treated by the NHS on your return. What exactly is the cooling-off period? At least two weeks between your decision and surgery, plus an offer of a second consultation beforehand. Nobody needs an urgent breast augmentation: if you are pressured to proceed or offered no cooling-off period, walk away. Are silicone implants safe? Implants are made from medical-grade silicone and have been used since the 1960s; the evidence suggests they are safe, and there is no association between breast augmentation and breast cancer. Rupture remains possible (about 1 in 10 at 10 years) and is usually treated by removal and exchange. Rare risks such as BIA-ALCL, and the symptoms described as breast implant illness, are covered above. What is the alternative to an implant? Lipofilling — transferring your own fat by liposuction and injection. It avoids an implant but usually needs several operations for a worthwhile effect, gives a gradual result and is variable. Your own fat is the only substance that should ever be injected into the breast. (3)Continuing Education ActivityStatPearls review section · Last updated 2023-07-18The review's opening summary: breast augmentation increases breast size, most often with an implant and less commonly with fat transfer, and is among the most commonly performed plastic surgery procedures in the United States. It frames the activity around indications, contraindications, complications and the role of the interprofessional team before and after surgery.Objectives are to identify the different techniques, describe the indications, review the complications and improve care coordination among the team.The FDA restricted silicone-filled implants for cosmetic enhancement from 1992; reconstructive patients continued to receive them after mastectomy.The activity is written for the interprofessional team involved in pre- and postoperative care.Read this section on ncbi.nlm.nih.gov →IntroductionStatPearls review section · Last updated 2023-07-18Breast augmentation is a surgical procedure in which breast size is enhanced, either by placing an implant or, less commonly, through fat transfer. The section traces FDA policy on silicone implants from the 1992 restriction to the 2006 reversal, describes the shift towards cohesive gel and form-stable implants, and sets out monitoring advice and the fact that implants are not permanent devices.Extensive research failed to confirm the disease fears that led to the 1992 silicone restriction, and the FDA allowed general use of silicone-filled implants again in 2006.By 2017 the majority of patients undergoing augmentation received cohesive gel silicone implants, with makers introducing different levels of gel firmness.The FDA recommends MRI screening every two years in patients with silicone implants to detect subclinical leaks, but adherence is incomplete and MRI readings can be false positive.Higher gel cohesion may lower rupture rates, but the review states that eventually all implants will rupture or break.Read this section on ncbi.nlm.nih.gov →Anatomy and PhysiologyStatPearls review section · Last updated 2023-07-18The anatomy relevant to augmentation: the breast sits on the anterior chest wall below the clavicle, bounded medially by the sternum, laterally by the latissimus dorsi and inferiorly by the inframammary fold, with the pectoralis muscles forming its posterior boundary.The inframammary fold is a dermal structure formed by fusion of the superficial and mammary fascia.Blood supply comes from the subdermal plexus with major contributions from the internal mammary artery, external mammary artery and intercostal perforators.Nerve supply is mainly through the intercostal plexus, with most contribution from the third to fifth intercostal nerves.Read this section on ncbi.nlm.nih.gov →Indications and contraindicationsWho the review says the procedure is for, and the conditions that should stop a surgeon from operating. (2)IndicationsStatPearls review section · Last updated 2023-07-18Implants are placed for reconstruction after mastectomy, for developmental disorders such as hypomastia, and for elective reasons related to self-image. Hypomastia may follow normal development or involution, especially after pregnancy, and people of all personality types may seek the procedure.Reported motivations include reconstruction, developmental under-development of the breast and elective enhancement of self-image.The review notes that when surveyed after surgery, the vast majority of women would undergo the operation again.Read this section on ncbi.nlm.nih.gov →ContraindicationsStatPearls review section · Last updated 2023-07-18Most patients have no contraindications, but the review lists the conditions that should prevent surgery and the patient factors that should pause it.Absolute reasons not to operate include active infection of the breast, active cancer and pregnancy.Relative reasons include a history of autoimmune disease, current radiation treatment, unstable medical conditions and known sensitivity to silicone.Psychological instability or unrealistic expectations are also given as reasons not to proceed.Read this section on ncbi.nlm.nih.gov →The operationEquipment, theatre team, preparation, implant choices, placement, incisions, anaesthesia, duration and expected recovery. (4)EquipmentStatPearls review section · Last updated 2023-07-18Routine operating-room equipment is usually sufficient. Extras depend on the approach: a lighted retractor or headlight for visualising the pocket, an endoscope for umbilical or axillary approaches, and sometimes an implant sleeve used as part of a no-touch technique.A no-touch technique limits handling of the implant to reduce implant trauma and bacterial contamination.Endoscopic equipment may be required when the umbilical or axillary route is used.Read this section on ncbi.nlm.nih.gov →PersonnelStatPearls review section · Last updated 2023-07-18The operating team normally consists of the surgeon, a scrubbed assistant, an anaesthesiologist and a circulating nurse working together in the operating room.Standard theatre roles apply: surgeon, scrubbed assistant, anaesthesiologist and circulating nurse.The team structure is described as the same as for other routine surgical procedures.Read this section on ncbi.nlm.nih.gov →PreparationStatPearls review section · Last updated 2023-07-18Patients are prepared for surgery as for any other surgical procedure, following the usual preoperative pathway.Preparation follows the routine preoperative work-up used for any operation, including assessment and consent.The review places emphasis on informed consent and on the pre-operative teaching that reduces later problems.Read this section on ncbi.nlm.nih.gov →Technique or TreatmentStatPearls review section · Last updated 2023-07-18Two main implant types are described, saline-filled and silicone-filled, both with a silicone outer shell that can be smooth or textured. a low-grade infection or biofilm is suspected as a cause, with Staphylococcus epidermidis and Cutibacterium acnes most commonly isolated.Complications Implant-associated lymphomaThe review reports a slim possibility that women with breast implants are more likely to be diagnosed with anaplastic large cell lymphoma (ALCL), possibly associated with a certain type of texturing, although the exact relationship has not been determined.Complications Reducing complicationsNurse-led preoperative instruction, stopping smoking, pharmacist allergy and medicines checks, and interprofessional follow-up are described as ways to lower complication rates, with earlier recognition improving outcomes.Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes Statements are paraphrased from the StatPearls review NBK482206, last updated 2023-07-18. It may occur naturally as in mammoplasia or may occur artificially through active intervention. Many women regard their breasts, which are female secondary sex characteristics, as important to their sexual attractiveness, as a sign of femininity that is important to their sense of self. Due to this, when a woman considers her breasts deficient in some respect, she might choose to engage in some activity intended to enhance them.Mammoplasia. The article names natural breast enlargement as mammoplasia, distinguishing it from enlargement produced by active intervention. Five types of surgical incision IncisionWhat the article says Inframammary incisionA cut at the inframammary fold (the bottom border of the breast) giving maximal access to the interior of the breast for precise pocket creation and implant placement. Scarring can be noticeable depending on skin type. Periareolar incisionA short (~5 cm) cut along the lower half of the areola's outer border. The narrow access makes large silicone implants harder to place, tends toward higher capsular contracture rates long term, and risks damaging milk ducts and nerves of the nipple-areola complex, which can impede breastfeeding. It also permits a concurrent breast lift. Transaxillary incisionA cut in the armpit with a tunnel under the skin to the breast pocket, done bluntly or with an endoscope. It avoids scarring the breast skin; the challenge is judging the ideal implant position for symmetry. Transumbilical incision (TUBA)An endoscopic approach through the navel, tunneling upward under the abdominal skin to place a saline implant. It avoids scarring the breast skin. Transabdominal incision (TABA)An endoscopic approach through the navel tunneling up to the breast pocket, performed while the patient simultaneously undergoes an abdominoplasty. Condensed from the “Types of surgical incision” section. The incision route is chosen with the surgeon according to anatomy, implant type and goals. Surgical technique Four implant-pocket placements Placements described in anatomical relation to the pectoralis major muscle. Four implant-pocket placements PlacementWhat the article says SubglandularThe implant sits between the breast tissue and the pectoralis major muscle (retromammary space), closest to the natural breast plane and usually the most aesthetic — but more prone to visible rippling in women with little soft tissue. SubfascialThe implant is placed beneath the fascia covering the pectoralis major muscle, to add size and volume for later contouring. Subpectoral (dual plane)The implant is placed beneath the pectoralis major muscle after partially releasing its lower attachments: the upper half of the implant is covered by muscle, the lower half sits in the subglandular plane. It maximizes upper coverage and lower expansion, at some risk of animation deformity (the implant moving with the muscle). SubmuscularThe implant is placed entirely beneath the pectoralis major muscle without cutting its lower origin; total coverage can be completed by releasing and reattaching lateral chest-wall muscles (serratus or pectoralis minor). Condensed from the “Implant-pocket placement” section. Placement affects coverage, rippling risk, recovery and how the implant moves. Implant types The four prosthesis types The four categories of breast prosthesis the article describes, two of which are discontinued. The four prosthesis types ProsthesisCategorySummaryDetail Saline breast prosthesisImplant typeA silicone-elastic shell filled with sterile saline solution in the operating room.First sold commercially by Laboratoires Arion of France in 1964. The empty shell is inserted through a short incision, then filled with saline and contoured for symmetry. Results are good to excellent, but rippling and wrinkling of the skin can show, especially in women with little breast tissue; with ample tissue and submuscular placement, results resemble those of silicone-gel implants. Silicone-gel breast prosthesisImplant typeA shell filled with viscous silicone gel; the technology has passed through five generations of design.Invented in 1961 by Frank Gerow and Thomas Cronin, made by Dow Corning, and first used in augmentation in 1962. Generation 1 (1963) was a teardrop silicone-rubber sack with a Dacron fastener patch. Generation 2 (1970s) used thin shells and low-cohesion gel — fragile, with higher rupture, leakage and capsular contracture rates that prompted class-action lawsuits; polyurethane-coated variants reduced contracture but were dropped in the U.S. over carcinogenic TDA by-products (they remain in use in Europe and South America); double-lumen designs combined gel and saline with post-operative volume adjustability. Generations 3 and 4 (1980s) added elastomer coatings to reduce gel bleed, with shaped, tapered and round textured or smooth models. Generation 5 (1990s) uses semi-solid cohesive gel that resists leakage and migration, with studies reporting lower capsular contracture and rupture rates than earlier generations. Alternative-composition breast prosthesisImplant type (discontinued)Fillers such as soy oil, polypropylene string, ox cartilage, Terylene wool, ground rubber, silastic or Teflon-silicone — now discontinued.The article lists these fillers as substances harmful to the body and no longer in use. Structured breast prosthesisImplant type (discontinued)Nested silicone-rubber shells with saline between them, approved by the FDA and Health Canada in 2014; now discontinued.Three nested shells support the upper half of the breast and the two spaces between them are filled with saline, combining saline and silicone technologies. The folded empty device is inserted, then filled with saline and the incision sutured. Condensed from the “Breast-augmentation prostheses” section. Breast Enlargement EducationBreast Enlargement: A Complete Guide to Surgical and Non-Surgical OptionsPublished 2026-10-28 · 4 min readAn evidence-aware guide to surgical and non-surgical breast enlargement options, limitations, safety and questions to ask.In this articleWhat breast enlargement meansSurgical optionsNon-surgical claims and limitsResults, longevity, risks and costQuestions for a surgeonWhat breast enlargement meansBreast enlargement can mean a change in volume, shape, projection, symmetry or simply the appearance of the chest in clothing. Natural breast size and shape vary with genetics, hormones, body weight, pregnancy, ageing and the balance of glandular and fatty tissue. A useful first step is defining the change you hope to see, because a procedure that changes projection is not automatically a procedure that creates durable volume.Surgical optionsImplant augmentation places a regulated medical device through an operation; silicone-gel and saline implants have different product characteristics, but neither should be described as a lifetime device. Fat transfer uses liposuction to collect and process a person’s own fat before grafting it to the breast. It can create a more modest volume change, but retained volume varies and future imaging should take the history of grafting into account.Non-surgical claims and limitsA supportive bra, padding, posture and styling can change appearance temporarily without changing breast tissue. Exercise strengthens the pectoral muscles beneath the breast but does not selectively grow breast tissue. Creams, supplements and massage have not shown a reliable, lasting increase in breast volume. Regulators warn against using injectable fillers or silicone to enlarge breasts.Results, longevity, risks and costHealing, sensation, scars, shape and longevity vary. Implant surgery can involve capsular contracture, rupture, infection, bleeding, changes in sensation and later operations. Fat transfer has its own risks, including uneven retention and fat necrosis. Pricing depends on clinician credentials, facility, anaesthesia, device or procedure choice, aftercare and the realistic possibility of future treatment; a low headline price is not a complete safety assessment.Questions for a surgeonAsk what is being proposed, why it fits your anatomy and goals, the product name and regulatory status, alternatives including doing nothing, the full cost, recovery plan, complication management, and expected long-term monitoring. A qualified clinician should welcome time to decide.Making sense of the information Start with the exact claimWhen reading about breast enlargement, separate a statement about appearance from a statement about anatomy, volume, safety or durability. Ask what was measured, for how long, in whom, and whether the same product, technique and body area are being discussed. A dramatic marketing image cannot answer those questions. This distinction is especially important where a procedure is described with broad terms such as “natural”, “non-invasive” or “advanced”. Plan for the whole decisionA procedure is more than the operation itself. Consider consultation time, health assessment, written consent, travel, support at home, follow-up, time away from work and the possibility that further treatment may be needed. Decisions made without room for questions, reflection or a second opinion deserve particular caution. Use reliable sourcesRegulator guidance, product instructions and peer-reviewed research answer different questions. A regulator may describe known risks and approved uses; a professional body may explain usual practice; a study may have limits in size, follow-up or relevance. No single source can decide individual suitability. If a claim cannot be traced to a credible source or a clinician cannot explain it plainly, treat that as a reason to pause. Keep expectations realisticPeople vary in anatomy, healing, scar formation, sensation, priorities and tolerance for risk. Even a technically uncomplicated procedure may involve discomfort, swelling, uncertainty during healing or a result that differs from an imagined picture. It is reasonable to ask what can go wrong, how it would be managed, and what the alternative is if the hoped-for change is not achieved. Protect your independenceTake notes, request written information and discuss the decision with someone you trust if that feels helpful. Be cautious about limited-time discounts, guaranteed results, pressure to pay a deposit immediately, or vague answers about who performs aftercare. Choosing no treatment, or postponing a decision, remains an appropriate option.Key takeawaysIndividual assessment matters more than generic online claims.Evidence, safety and realistic expectations should guide decisions.Taking time and choosing no treatment are valid options.Sources and further readingU.S. FDA: Breast implantsNHS: Breast enlargementASPS: Breast augmentationRelated articlesBreast Implants vs Fat Transfer — Which Option Is Right for You?Non-Surgical Breast Enlargement — What Actually Works?Breast Augmentation Recovery — Week-by-Week Expectations Frequently asked questions Is this article medical advice? No. It is general education and cannot assess your health, anatomy, goals or suitability. Can a result be guaranteed? No. Results, risks, healing and the need for future care vary between individuals. Who should I speak to? Discuss individual questions with an appropriately qualified, registered clinician. Where can I check evidence? Use the linked regulator and professional-body sources, and ask for product-specific information. What is the safest next step? Take time, compare reliable information, and do not proceed under pressure. Use information to prepare your questions This educational article cannot assess individual suitability. Discuss any treatment decision with an appropriately qualified clinician. Breast Enlargement EducationBreast Augmentation Recovery — Week-by-Week ExpectationsPublished 2026-10-25 · 3 min readA week-by-week educational overview of breast augmentation recovery, aftercare, restrictions and warning signs.In this articleBefore surgery and the first 48 hoursWeek 1Weeks 2 to 4Weeks 4 to 6 and beyondUrgent warning signsBefore surgery and the first 48 hoursArrange support, transport and a clear written recovery plan. In the first day or two, discomfort, fatigue, swelling and limited movement are common, but the treating surgeon’s instructions take priority over any general timeline.Week 1Support garments, medications, wound care, showering and sleeping instructions differ by technique. Many people need practical help and time away from normal tasks. Do not drive or return to work simply because a calendar says it is time.Weeks 2 to 4Bruising and swelling may improve while tightness, altered sensation and unevenness still evolve. Follow-up appointments are a chance to review healing and ask about work, arm movement and exercise.Weeks 4 to 6 and beyondSome activities may resume gradually only with clearance. Scars continue to mature for months, and final settling takes longer than early photographs suggest. Avoid comparing your healing to online timelines.Urgent warning signsContact the treating team urgently for worsening pain, sudden swelling, spreading redness, fever, pus-like drainage, shortness of breath, chest pain or any concern you were told to report.Making sense of the information Start with the exact claimWhen reading about breast augmentation recovery , separate a statement about appearance from a statement about anatomy, volume, safety or durability. Ask what was measured, for how long, in whom, and whether the same product, technique and body area are being discussed. A dramatic marketing image cannot answer those questions. This distinction is especially important where a procedure is described with broad terms such as “natural”, “non-invasive” or “advanced”. Plan for the whole decisionA procedure is more than the operation itself. Consider consultation time, health assessment, written consent, travel, support at home, follow-up, time away from work and the possibility that further treatment may be needed. Decisions made without room for questions, reflection or a second opinion deserve particular caution. Use reliable sourcesRegulator guidance, product instructions and peer-reviewed research answer different questions. A regulator may describe known risks and approved uses; a professional body may explain usual practice; a study may have limits in size, follow-up or relevance. No single source can decide individual suitability. If a claim cannot be traced to a credible source or a clinician cannot explain it plainly, treat that as a reason to pause. Keep expectations realisticPeople vary in anatomy, healing, scar formation, sensation, priorities and tolerance for risk. Even a technically uncomplicated procedure may involve discomfort, swelling, uncertainty during healing or a result that differs from an imagined picture. It is reasonable to ask what can go wrong, how it would be managed, and what the alternative is if the hoped-for change is not achieved. Protect your independenceTake notes, request written information and discuss the decision with someone you trust if that feels helpful. Be cautious about limited-time discounts, guaranteed results, pressure to pay a deposit immediately, or vague answers about who performs aftercare. Choosing no treatment, or postponing a decision, remains an appropriate option.Key takeawaysIndividual assessment matters more than generic online claims.Evidence, safety and realistic expectations should guide decisions.Taking time and choosing no treatment are valid options.Sources and further readingU.S. FDA: Breast implantsNHS: Breast enlargementASPS: Breast augmentationRelated articlesBreast Enlargement: A Complete Guide to Surgical and Non-Surgical OptionsBreast Implants vs Fat Transfer — Which Option Is Right for You?Non-Surgical Breast Enlargement — What Actually Works? No. Results, risks, healing and the need for future care vary between individuals. Who should I speak to? Discuss individual questions with an appropriately qualified, registered clinician. Where can I check evidence? Use the linked regulator and professional-body sources, and ask for product-specific information. What is the safest next step? Ask what was measured, for how long, in whom, and whether the same product, technique and body area are being discussed. A dramatic marketing image cannot answer those questions. No single source can decide individual suitability. If a claim cannot be traced to a credible source or a clinician cannot explain it plainly, treat that as a reason to pause. Keep expectations realisticPeople vary in anatomy, healing, scar formation, sensation, priorities and tolerance for risk. Even a technically uncomplicated procedure may involve discomfort, swelling, uncertainty during healing or a result that differs from an imagined picture. It is reasonable to ask what can go wrong, how it would be managed, and what the alternative is if the hoped-for change is not achieved. Home/Privacy policy Who we areThis website is an independent, educational publication about breast enlargement. It is not a clinic and does not provide medical services. The contact-form endpoint validates the message and, only when delivery is configured, sends it through Resend to the published mailbox. Information is not sold or used for advertising or marketing.Retention and legal basisWe have not been given a fixed retention schedule for the publisher’s mailbox. Messages may remain in that mailbox or the delivery provider’s systems for as long as needed to handle the enquiry, meet legal obligations or resolve a dispute. Where a privacy law requires a legal basis, processing is based on your request to receive a reply and, where required, the consent you provide by submitting the form. This general notice does not replace jurisdiction-specific legal advice.Your choicesYou may ask for access to, correction of, or deletion of information you submitted by emailing enquiries@nonsurgicalbreastenlargement.in. We may need enough information to identify the enquiry, and legal or technical limits can affect what can be deleted. The publisher has not supplied a jurisdiction-specific list of privacy rights, so this page does not make one.Cookies and analyticsThe published site does not intentionally set analytics, advertising or marketing cookies, and it does not include a consent-management banner because no non-essential cookies are currently used. If analytics, advertising pixels or embedded third-party media are added later, this policy and any required consent controls must be updated before they are activated.
